name: MATHVISTA
description: MATHVISTA is a benchmark designed to evaluate mathematical reasoning of foundation models in visual contexts. It consists of 6,141 examples derived from 28 existing multimodal datasets involving mathematics and 3 newly created datasets (IQTest, FunctionQA, and PaperQA). The benchmark covers seven mathematical reasoning types (algebraic, arithmetic, geometry, logical, numeric commonsense, scientific, and statistical reasoning) and five primary tasks (figure question answering, geometry problem solving, math word problem, textbook question answering, and visual question answering) across diverse visual contexts including natural images, geometry diagrams, abstract scenes, synthetic scenes, charts, and plots.
creator: Pan Lu, Hritik Bansal, Tony Xia, Jiacheng Liu, Chunyuan Li, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Hao Cheng, Kai-Wei Chang, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao (UCLA, University of Washington, Microsoft Research)
citeAs: Pan Lu et al., MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts, ICLR 2024.
rai:dataCollection: MATHVISTA was collected by: (1) collecting nine MathQA datasets in multimodal settings; (2) reviewing more than 70 VQA datasets and collecting 19 that contain math-related instances and are publicly available; and (3) creating three new datasets (IQTest, FunctionQA, PaperQA). For VQA datasets, heuristic rules were designed to automatically select examples likely to involve mathematical reasoning, followed by expert annotation. Each source dataset was limited to up to 400 examples to ensure balanced representation.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Only 85.6% of examples (5,261 out of 6,141) have annotations, as annotations were sourced from original data providers. Due to the heterogeneity of these sources, annotations lack a unified format and structure.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Data was sourced from 28 existing multimodal datasets (9 MathQA datasets and 19 VQA datasets) and 3 newly created datasets. IQTest examples were sourced from puzzle test figures on online learning platforms. FunctionQA examples were based on functional plots. PaperQA examples were sourced from papers released in August 2023 on Huggingface (https://huggingface.co/papers).
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: PaperQA sourced from papers released in August 2023; Multimodal Bard evaluation dates range from Sep 8, 2023 to Sep 10, 2023; GPT-4V evaluation dates range from Oct 7, 2023 to Oct 15, 2023.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For VQA datasets, heuristic rules were used to automatically select examples likely to involve mathematical reasoning: examples with numeric answers or those containing quantity words in the questions were selected. Each source dataset was limited to up to 400 examples. For the testmini subset (1,000 examples), a sampling strategy was adopted: (1) randomly sample questions with a threshold number of 4 for each source dataset; (2) randomly sample the remaining questions for each source dataset based on its proportion in the entire set.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For VQA datasets, automatic filtration using heuristic rules yielded 4,949 VQA-format examples. Three expert annotators then manually labeled these examples to determine if they involve mathematical reasoning, using majority voting to finalize selections. Coarse labels of mathematical reasoning were automatically obtained from source dataset details. Expert annotators manually verified 1,000 examples for mathematical reasoning categories, finding 94.1% exact match with automatic annotations. Several quality checks were conducted to address unidentified errors.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: For the three new datasets (IQTest, FunctionQA, PaperQA), all questions were manually annotated by graduate students in STEM fields and refined through a rigorous review process. A two-step process was used: each dataset was independently annotated by three reviewers, achieving a 99.2% inter-annotation consistency rate; discrepancies (6 out of 736 questions) were resolved through discussion among the entire review team. For VQA mathematical reasoning labeling, annotators were trained with detailed instructions and examples, with three labeling options (Yes, No, Unsure). For metadata annotation, expert annotators manually labeled mathematical reasoning categories for 1,000 examples. Human performance baseline was established using Amazon Mechanical Turk with qualified annotators (high school diploma or higher, >5,000 HIT tasks completed, acceptance score >0.99).
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Custom annotation tool (GUI shown in paper figures); Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) for human performance baseline and Multimodal Bard assessment task
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Inter-annotator agreement for VQA mathematical reasoning labeling was measured using Fleiss Kappa score of 0.775, indicating substantial consistency. For the three new datasets, inter-annotation consistency rate was 99.2% (only 6 out of 736 questions had disagreements). For automatic mathematical reasoning category annotation, 94.1% of examples had exact same set of reasoning types between automatic and human annotations, and 98.79% of individual labels were identical.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The answer labels for the test set will not be publicly released to prevent data contamination; an online evaluation platform will be maintained. The benchmark is part of an ongoing research process with commitment to maintaining datasets (refining potential data noise) in response to community feedback. The leaderboard will evolve in response to new models. Future iterations will encompass broader problems, visual contexts, and unified comprehensive annotations.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset includes images of people (some models like Multimodal Bard refused to respond to images of people). Human annotator demographics collected include highest level of educational attainment (high school diploma or higher required). AMT workers' task history and acceptance scores were used for qualification.
rai:dataSocialImpact: MATHVISTA is designed to facilitate the development of AI agents capable of tackling mathematically intensive and visually rich real-world tasks, with applications in educational disciplines, logical queries about statistical data, theorem proving, and scientific discovery. The benchmark highlights significant gaps between current AI models and human performance, underscoring the need for improvements in mathematical reasoning with visual comprehension.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset's focus on mathematical reasoning within visual contexts spanning specific domains like science and college-level math may limit generalizability. The dataset contains 6.57% non-English questions (Chinese and Persian), which may introduce language bias. Human performance baseline required high school diploma or higher, which may not represent all demographics. The benchmark may have gaps in representation of certain types of mathematical problems and visuals.
rai:dataLimitations: While MATHVISTA encompasses a broad spectrum of tasks and visual contexts, there may be gaps in representation of certain types of mathematical problems and visuals. The scalability and generalizability to other domains remain a concern. Annotations lack unified format and structure due to heterogeneous sources. Only 85.6% of examples have annotations. The benchmark focused exclusively on the most recent and prominent models at time of publication. Current models struggle particularly with logical reasoning (GPT-4V achieves only 21.6% accuracy) and complex figure understanding.
rai:dataUseCases: Testing and evaluation of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) on mathematical reasoning in visual contexts. The testmini subset (1,000 examples) is intended for model development validation or for those with limited computing resources. The test set (5,141 examples) is for standard evaluation. Not recommended for training due to potential data contamination concerns (test labels not released).
